title: Correos: formal emails
_note: business-spanish run, 2026-11-07: written by hand for Spain, not yet read by a human. Words already in the lexicon or another deck are refs, with a work example and sense; deHint = German translation (the 'German' tab).
intro: A work email in Spain has a clear frame: a greeting with a colon, the reason you are writing, what you need, a closing line and your name. This unit gives you the phrases for each step, two model emails and practice in choosing the right tone. Use usted with clients, suppliers and public offices until they move to tú. Among colleagues, tú is normal.
introEasy: Do you write emails at work? Learn how to start, what to say and how to finish.

models.title: To a client: sending a quote
models.text:
Asunto: Presupuesto de la reforma de la oficina

Estimada señora Ortega:

Le escribo en relación con su solicitud del 12 de mayo. Le adjunto el presupuesto de la reforma de la oficina, con el desglose por partidas.

El precio incluye los materiales y la mano de obra, pero no el IVA. Podríamos empezar la obra el 3 de junio, siempre que nos confirme el pedido antes del 20 de mayo.

Para cualquier duda, estoy a su disposición.

Quedo a la espera de su respuesta.

Un cordial saludo,

Luis Romero
Reformas Ibáñez, S. L.
notes: Spanish puts a colon after the greeting, where English has a comma. The next line starts with a capital letter.
Everything stays in the usted form: le adjunto, su solicitud, nos confirme. Mixing tú and usted in one email looks careless.
Siempre que (as long as) takes the subjunctive: siempre que nos confirme.
Months take a small letter: el 12 de mayo. El desglose por partidas is the breakdown, item by item. S. L. is a limited company.
The IVA is Spanish VAT. A quote should say whether its price includes it.

models.title: To a colleague: a change of plan
models.text:
Asunto: Cambio de hora de la reunión

Hola, Marta:

Te escribo porque la reunión del jueves pasa de las diez a las doce: el cliente no puede venir antes. ¿Te viene bien?

Te reenvío su correo y te adjunto el orden del día. Si falta algo, dímelo y lo añado.

Gracias y un saludo,

Adil
notes: Same frame, lighter tone: tú forms (te escribo, te adjunto, dímelo), but still a greeting, a subject line and a sign-off.
¿Te viene bien? (does that suit you?) is the everyday way to check a time. With a client: ¿Le viene bien?
The subject line says what the email is about in a few words. Una reunión alone tells your colleague nothing.

tips: Don't translate «Dear» as «Querido» at work: querido is for family and friends. «Estimado» is the safe choice.
If you don't know the person's name, write «Buenos días:» or «Estimados señores:». Spanish has no fixed equivalent of «To whom it may concern» for everyday emails.
Spanish has usted and tú: look at how the other person writes to you and do the same. When they sign with only their first name, tú is usually welcome.

words.example: Le envío un correo electrónico con los detalles.
Escribe un asunto claro: «Factura de febrero».
Compruebe el remitente antes de abrir el archivo.
Falta un destinatario en este correo.
No puedo abrir el archivo adjunto.
Te reenvío el correo del cliente.
Puse a la jefa en copia oculta.
Le ruego que me envíe un acuse de recibo.
La factura vence a final de mes.
Añade tu cargo a la firma del correo.

translations.en: to thank for, to be grateful for

words.example: Tenemos una factura pendiente de pago.

exercises.context: To a client you have never met.
exercises.explain: Estimada is the safe formal greeting. Querida is for family and friends, and hola with a surname sounds odd.
Spanish uses a colon after the greeting. A comma there is copied from English.

exercises.prompt: Le escribo ___ relación con su pedido.
exercises.explain: The fixed phrase is en relación con (regarding).
I am the one sending it, so the yo form. Le means to you (usted).

exercises.prompt: Le agradecería que me ___ la fecha.
exercises.explain: After a conditional like agradecería, que takes the imperfect subjunctive.

exercises.prompt: Quedo a la ___ de su respuesta.
exercises.explain: Quedo a la espera de is the standard closing line. Esperanza means hope.
La demora is the delay. You can also say el retraso, with el.

exercises.context: You are writing to your whole team.
exercises.explain: Os is to you all (vosotros). Te is one person, and le is one person you call usted.

es419.note: Spain's os: Latin America says les here.

exercises.context: The end of an email to a colleague.
exercises.explain: Gracias y un saludo is friendly and professional, and it suits most colleagues.

exercises.context: The end of a formal letter to a public office.
exercises.explain: Atentamente is the most formal sign-off. Un abrazo is for people you know well.
El asunto is the subject line. El sujeto is a false friend: the subject of a sentence.
Lamentamos las molestias: we apologise for the inconvenience. Disculpas are what you offer: pedimos disculpas.
